source_read: PDF pp. 1–4 (all pages; Table 1 on p. 2 checked on the rendered page); supplementary materials not read

claims.overstatement: None. The claim reads the 6-month result correctly ('not clearly different'), unlike the abstract's conclusion, which speaks of declines 'at six and 12 months'. One precision: 'the share using strips at each survey is not printed' holds for the article, but the Methods say descriptive statistics for every wave are in the supplementary materials (not read), so the shares may exist there.
claims.note: All numbers match Table 1 and the text: 12 months 0.642 (0.447–0.923) and 0.557 (0.364–0.853); 6 months 0.936 (0.696–1.258) and 0.946 (0.650–1.375); 541 people/1081 observations and 212/636; lifetime use 65.1%, 77.8%, 79.7%; 213 with no follow-up (541 − 328), 213/541 = 39.4%; 54.3% vs 65.1% compares the 213 with the 212 complete cases (not with everyone followed up). Recruitment dates June 2021 to March 2022 are baseline dates. The model also shows a calendar-time decline (later enrolment, aOR 0.793 per quarter) and a steeper fall among women (p < .05 at both follow-ups), neither of which the claim needs. Why use fell was not measured; the authors' explanation is interpretation.

anchors.extracted: Past-30-day FTS use vs baseline, mixed-effects logistic regression: full sample (541 people, 1081 observations) 6 months aOR 0.936 (0.696–1.258), 12 months 0.642 (0.447–0.923), p < .05; complete cases (212, 636 observations) 0.946 (0.650–1.375) and 0.557 (0.364–0.853), p < .01.
Decline over 12 months in both samples (0.642; 0.557); later enrolment associated with less use in the full sample (aOR per quarter 0.793, p < .01).
541 completed baseline, 328 at least one follow-up, 212 both (complete cases); among complete cases, lifetime FTS use 65.1% at baseline, 77.8% at 6 months, 79.7% at 12 months.

Attrition could bias estimates; the 213 with no follow-up were less often married or living as married and unhoused, less often had witnessed an overdose (56.8% vs 69.8%) and less often had used FTS (54.3% vs 65.1%) than complete cases; convenience sample at two rural SSPs.
Authors' interpretation, not measured: once fentanyl is the expected opioid, testing for it adds little; lower use reflects reduced informational value rather than unwillingness to check drugs.
Descriptive statistics at all survey waves, gender-interaction results and attrition statistics are in the supplementary materials.
Abstract speaks of declines at six and 12 months, although the 6-month estimates are not significant (CIs include 1).

claims.overstatement: None for the Erickson sentence. For the lead sentence: this study does not show more fentanyl use (aOR 1.332, 0.948–1.872, as the claim states) or more injecting among strip users; everyone injected (eligibility), and injections per day were not associated (1.009, 0.991–1.027). '(2021 to 2023)': baseline June 2021 to March 2022 with 6- and 12-month follow-ups; the end date of follow-up is not printed.
claims.note: All six full-sample odds ratios match Table 1. They come from one mixed-effects model and are adjusted for one another and for wave, enrolment timing, age, sex, race, education, state and other drug use; time-varying covariates mean they mix within- and between-person differences. Complete-case results are similar (witnessed 2.257, heroin 1.891, married 1.608, unhoused 0.611). Self-reported surveys; recruited by direct intercept at two SSPs.

anchors.extracted: Past-30-day FTS use, aOR (95% CI): witnessed overdose past 6 months 2.444 (1.784–3.347); heroin past 30 days 1.615 (1.107–2.357); married or living as married 1.521 (1.084–2.134); currently unhoused 0.679 (0.504–0.913); own overdose past 6 months 0.981 (0.676–1.424); fentanyl past 30 days 1.332 (0.948–1.872); injections per day 1.009 (0.991–1.027).

Witnessing an overdose strongly associated with use (2.444; complete cases 2.257); heroin use 1.615 (complete cases 1.891); unhoused lower odds (0.679; 0.611); married higher (1.521); no significant association with fentanyl use, access to heroin or own overdose.

People who inject drugs purposively recruited at SSPs in North Carolina and West Virginia by direct intercept; eligible if injected in past 30 days; model with wave fixed effects, time-invariant covariates, a person-level random intercept and time-varying covariates (housing, past-30-day drug use, injections per day, overdose, witnessing, preferences, access to heroin).

key_findings.note: The same sentence (p. 3) also says those lost were less likely to be unhoused; the card's attrition field notes this, the key finding leaves it out.

reporting_issues.note: Found independently in step 1: the complete-case column's witnessed-overdose (65.1%) and fentanyl-preference (26.4%) values are the 12-month values in the text.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E, high overall, driven by unmeasured confounding (service contact, strip supply) and 39% attrition related to the outcome. Domain judgments are consistent with the worst-domain rule.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the abstract's six-month decline, the 'key motivator' causal reading, and 'across all demographic groups' (only gender examined) go beyond the results.

missed.finding: Injections per day (aOR 1.009, 0.991–1.027; complete cases 0.979) and methamphetamine use (1.083) were not associated with FTS use. Not in the key findings; relevant to the lead of cl_dc_uptake_who_tests ('more injecting'), which this study does not support. Everyone injected, so only frequency could differ.
